content:
Gene therapy aims to treat disease by adding, changing or switching off genetic material in cells. Researchers are exploring whether it could reduce joint inflammation or protect cartilage.

This guide gives a cautious overview of where things stand. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Why gene therapy is being studied

Researchers are testing ways to deliver genes into joints so that cells make helpful proteins, for example to reduce inflammation or pain.

Where research stands

  • Most work is in laboratories or early, small human trials.
  • Long-term safety and benefit are not yet known.
  • Gene therapy is not offered as standard NHS treatment for arthritis.

Be cautious of unproven treatments

Some clinics advertise gene, stem cell or other unproven treatments. These may be costly and may not be safe. Ask your GP or rheumatology team before considering any treatment.

Taking part in research

You can search for UK studies on NIHR Be Part of Research or ask your rheumatology team.

What helps now

Established treatments include exercise, weight management, pain relief and, for inflammatory arthritis, disease-modifying medicines.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I get gene therapy for arthritis on the NHS?

It is not a standard treatment. It may only be available within research studies.

Should I pay for treatment abroad?

Discuss it with your doctor first. Unproven treatments can carry risks.

Sources and further reading

  • NIHR Be Part of Research
